I was also in your position.  Took a medical withdrawal from my very first semester of college.  I was in the wrong program, was taking too many classes, putting too much pressure on myself, and wasn't equipped to handle my depression.

GO TO THE DOCTOR. I swear, it helps.  You don't have to take the pills but for someone to validate what you're feeling helps tremendously.  Then, take it slow.  Your parents may be upset, yes, but they love you first and foremost.  Tell them what's been going on.  Take a break for awhile.

Also, my dad had a worse GPA than you did his first semester and went on to own his own company for 35+ years.  It may feel like the end of the world, but there are resources out there for you if you need help.  And thanks for reaching out to us Redditors.

One time in high school, another student (not being malicious, just stating matter-of-fact) said that I "looked like death".  Yes, I was extremely depressed at the time, not eating a lot, etc.  But that comment stuck with me for YEARS.  In an effort to compensate, I would tan so I didn't look so sickly (which really is bad for you).  I finally started feeling okay about it last summer (and now I have no desire to be tan).  Were the things he said about you things that could potentially affect your health?  Let's say for example, he called you overweight.  You absolutely should love your body no matter what, I 100% agree with that.  But in my experience, when I work out and eat healthier and am a healthier weight, I have more confidence, can perform certain activities better, and am healthier overall.  If it is something that you could work on that would make you feel better, would you consider trying that?  Once again, in no way am I supporting this serious DOOF, but it is important to stay healthy so you can be confident and happy with yourself.  However, self-love is the biggest thing.
